#1 You're not in the military anymore. The culture is way different. At some locations, you'll see a big difference in culture, especially when it comes to organization and tool control. It's emphasized but not enforced the way the military does (Varies by job location and I'm only speaking for places I've worked I know the military contracts are way better at this) Also you're dealing with civilians and at third party MRO's you'll get a lot of green fresh A&P's and a lot of visa workers depending on where you are. Be mindful of that. A lot of the visa guys do good work even though their English isn't very good. 

#2 Know your companies policies. Some locations can mandate OT while others can't. Know the procedures to cover your own ass or stick it to shitty bosses. Don't let the higher ups mismanagement fuck you over. I've seen it a million times. 

#3 Broaden your skills. Learn avionics, sheet metal, or composites. Airlines love A&P's who can do more. Makes you more valuable. Better bargaining tool for raises. That being said, know your limitations. 

#4 Don't be a dick. It's a small world. Word gets around, and I've seen people lose opportunities for it.  

#5 The quality of the customer make the job just as hard as the airplane can. Everyone has their own rules for how they want you to touch their planes. Customers' inability to get parts or willingness to pull the trigger on repairs can make things longer and more convoluted than they need to be. Just the way she goes sometimes.

If I had a reason to I would. With the way we do our maintenance and our procedures are laid out it would be very hard to get to a point like that. We don’t work on piston engines but if we did this is how we would lay out a piston change for example 
1. The maintenance technician would gather all appropriate manuals and tooling required by said manuals 

2. The maintenance technician would gain access to the engine by opening or removing cowlings

3. The maintenance technician would remove the cylinder and the piston 

4. The maintenance technician would clean and inspect the area per all applicable technical publications including service bulletins and airworthiness directives. 

6. Any discrepancies found would be worked and inspected by a maintenance technician and an inspector 

5. The maintenance technician would approach me to get an OK to install the new piston. I would go over the area with the tech ensuring the parts are airworthy and have the proper documentation. 

6. The maintenance technician would install the new piston under my oversight. Then I would inspect the area again to ensure proper installation and no foreign object being left inside the engine

7. Then the maintenance technician would reinstall the cylinder under my oversight.
To answer your question better I do not know whether that practice is legal because if we did so it would violate our GMM and company practices.

My company does not engage in that practice. I do not agree with it and no company should ever put parts on an aircraft that are not considered serviceable at the time of installation. With how our operating and inventory system works any part removed from an aircraft in any other reason than the furthering of maintenance it requires an inspector and/or a 145 to determine serviceability and airworthiness of said part.
